legend.name: Ash cloud
legend.meaning: Gas and tiny bits of shattered rock

steps.title: Volcano
steps.instruction: Trace the volcano and its crater.

note.text: Steep volcanoes like Mount St. Helens are built of layers of lava and ash. Most stand near subduction zones.

steps.title: Magma chamber
steps.instruction: Trace the magma chamber deep below.

note.text: Magma collects in a chamber kilometres underground. Under Mount St. Helens it's about 6 to 14 km down.
note.remember: Magma chamber: the store of melted rock.

steps.title: Vent
steps.instruction: Trace the vent rising to the crater.

note.text: Magma rises through the vent and erupts from the crater at the top.
Gas-rich magma can erupt explosively, blasting ash high into the sky.

steps.title: Warning: earthquakes
steps.instruction: Draw the two zigzags for small earthquakes.

note.text: Hundreds of small earthquakes show magma moving underground. Seismometers detect them.
note.remember: Swarms of small quakes are a warning.

steps.title: Warning: bulge
steps.instruction: Draw the bulge swelling out of the volcano's side.

note.text: A volcano swells as magma pushes up. Tiltmeters and GPS measure it. Rising gas is another warning sign.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: Color the magma and the ash cloud.

steps.title: Name the parts
steps.instruction: Pick the name for each numbered part.

mistakes.Crater: The crater is the bowl at the top. This pipe leading up to it is the vent.

steps.title: Forecast
steps.question: Which set of readings would most strongly suggest an eruption is coming?

options.text: Many small earthquakes, the side swelling, and more gas
options.feedback: Yes. Together they show magma rising and pressure building, so scientists can warn people to leave.
Weather doesn't tell us about magma. Scientists watch quakes, swelling and gas.

options.text: No change at all for years
options.feedback: No change suggests the magma isn't moving. Changes are the warning signs.
Snow is weather. The warning signs are quakes, swelling and gas.

steps.title: Hazards compared
steps.question: Why can scientists often forecast volcanic eruptions but not earthquakes on a fault?

options.text: Eruptions usually give warning signs first; most big earthquakes strike suddenly
options.feedback: Right. Rising magma causes quakes, swelling and gas before an eruption. Fault earthquakes rarely give such warnings.
Not never, but usually there are signs. Fault earthquakes rarely give any.
Earthquakes can be very destructive. They're just much harder to predict.
They do, closely. But most earthquakes still strike with no notice.
